quickVerdict: Freshchat is the better default choice for almost any team: at a similar or lower entry price, it gives you nine-plus native channels (WhatsApp, Instagram, SMS, and more) against Olark's essentially single-channel web chat, plus a far more generous free tier. Olark is worth it specifically if you want the simplest possible chat box with zero interest in social channels and value its long, dependable track record — sixteen years of one company doing one thing. Most teams outgrow single-channel chat quickly, which is why channel breadth usually decides this comparison before AI or pricing details do.
tldr: Olark is a 2009-era website live chat tool that has stayed narrow by design — a chat console and now an AI website agent, with no real presence outside the web widget. Freshchat is Freshworks' messaging product, natively covering nine-plus channels including WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger, and SMS in one inbox.

Pricing looks similar at a glance but tells different stories: Olark's classic seat is $29/agent/mo (down to $19 on a two-year commit); Freshchat is $0 free for up to 10 agents, then $19/agent/mo on Growth — cheaper than Olark's discounted rate while including far more channels.

Both bolt AI on as a separately-priced add-on rather than including it — Olark's AI Website Agent costs a flat $400/month billed annually with one seat included, while Freshchat's Freddy AI Agent is metered at $49 per 100 sessions on top of seat costs.

Freshchat's AI is more capable on paper: Freddy AI Agent takes documented actions against Shopify, Stripe, PayPal, and FedEx, while Olark's Aiden agent is scoped to answering from site content and documents only, with no order-lookup capability found anywhere in its documentation.

Olark's real strength is a long, dependable track record on the chat console itself — independent reviewers give it a 4.7/5 ease-of-use sub-score and describe multi-year runs without outages. Freshchat's strength is breadth, though it carries its own reliability complaints, including a documented 13-day outage.

Pick Freshchat if you need more than one channel or want AI that can actually take action. Pick Olark if your needs are genuinely just a simple, dependable web chat box and you want the lowest-friction classic seat available.

verdict: This comparison is really a channel-count decision wearing a pricing comparison's clothes. Olark has done one thing since 2009 — a dependable web chat console — and it does that thing well enough that independent reviewers give it a 4.7/5 ease-of-use sub-score and casually mention five-plus years without outages. But it is genuinely narrow: no native WhatsApp, Instagram, or SMS on the current product (those are tagged 'Olark Classic,' the legacy line), and its AI website agent, however sensibly built, cannot look up an order or touch a business system on the evidence available. Freshchat starts from the opposite assumption — that support lives across nine-plus channels — and prices that breadth at $19/agent on Growth, actually cheaper than Olark's discounted long-term rate, with a free tier that covers up to 10 agents against Olark's 20-chats-a-month ceiling. Freshchat's AI is also the more capable of the two on paper: Freddy AI Agent takes documented actions against Shopify, Stripe, PayPal, and FedEx, where Olark's Aiden is confined to answering questions from content. Neither company includes its AI in the seat price — Olark's is a blunt $400/month annual commitment with one seat bundled in, while Freshchat's $49-per-100-sessions model at least lets you start small and see what usage actually costs. Both have real, specific reliability complaints on record, so don't assume Freshchat's breadth comes risk-free: a documented 13-day outage and push-notification failures show up in its review base just as outage-free multi-year runs show up in Olark's. My honest read: unless your support volume is genuinely confined to your website and you have no interest in messaging channels, Freshchat's channel breadth and lower entry price make it the harder one to justify passing up. Olark earns its place only for teams that have already decided they want the simplest possible tool and nothing more.
